query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small reactive alloying addition (e.g., ~1–2 at.% Ti) into the CoCrFeNi matrix will induce the in‐situ formation of finely dispersed nanoprecipitates that generate a nanohierarchical microstructure. This dual‐phase structure will enable an adaptive friction interface protection mechanism that lowers both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate across a sliding temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy produced by standard melting and thermo-mechanical processing (e.g. cold rolling and annealing) with a homogeneous FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying modification by adding a controlled amount (approximately 1–2 at.%) of Ti into the CoCrFeNi composition. The processing route would include melting with the added Ti followed by a heat treatment designed to promote the nucleation of nano‐sized precipitates and grain refinement.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in air over a temperature range from room temperature (RT) up to 800 °C, under a moderate normal load (e.g., ~5–20 N) and sliding speeds typical of laboratory tribometers.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered nanohierarchical microstructure characterized by nano-coupled grains in the matrix and uniformly dispersed nanoprecipitates. At lower temperatures the fine structure mediates stress relaxation through multiple deformation pathways, while at elevated temperatures these precipitates promote the timely formation of a nanocrystalline, lubricious oxide (glaze) layer.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, the enhanced grain boundary and nanoprecipitate network helps in distributing frictional stress and inhibits severe plastic deformation, leading to lower friction. At high temperature, the reactive Ti-rich nanoprecipitates oxidize to form a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer that reduces adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby maintaining low friction and wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi, the Ti-alloyed variant is expected to achieve a lower average friction coefficient and a wear rate reduced by up to 1–2 orders of magnitude across the full sliding temperature range.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a conventional, single-phase FCC microstructure and no engineered nano-coupled features.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under ambient air conditions, with sliding tests performed under loads of approximately 5–20 N and temperatures ranging from RT to 800 °C. Effects outside this temperature range or under highly aggressive chemical environments have not been tested.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in friction coefficient and wear rate are uncertain until experimental validation; potential interactions between added Ti and other alloying elements under prolonged high-temperature exposure may also influence long-term stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the baseline CoCrFeNi HEA and (b) the modified CoCrFeNi + 1–2 at.% Ti alloy processed using identical melting, thermomechanical processing, and annealing conditions to achieve similar grain sizes. Both sets will be subjected to sliding wear tests in air on a reciprocating tribometer at controlled loads (e.g., 10 N) with the temperature systematically varied from room temperature to 800 °C.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) as a function of temperature
Wear volume or specific wear rate measured by profilometry or weight loss
Post-test surface characterization (SEM, EDS) to verify formation of a nanocrystalline glaze layer in the Ti-modified alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant decrease in both the COF and wear rate (by at least an order of magnitude improvement at high temperatures compared to baseline) or if the expected adaptive glaze layer is not observed, then the hypothesis that the engineered nanohierarchical microstructure provides adaptive friction interface protection would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

To overcome the aforementioned shortcomings, we offer an alternative approach for fabricating high temperature wear resistant HEA coatings on H13 hot working die steel. The introduction of W in the AlCoCrFeNi HEA system provides a potential solution for high temperature application because of its high melting point, low coefficient of thermal expansion, and good creep resistance [,]. More specifically, the introduction of W does not change the original phase composition of HEA []. Therefore, the performance of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is expected to be enhanced via introducing W particles. In this work, the AlCoCrFeNiWx (x = 0, 0.5 and 1) HEA coatings were fabricated by laser cladding on hot working die steel. The morphology of the microstructure and chemical composition of micro-areas were investigated in detail. The wear resistance of the coatings was tested at a high temperature, and then the wear mechanism of the worn surfaces was analyzed. We proved that the microstructure becomes more stable and enhances wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA on H13 steel by the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetal
